chapter: Desvigne, Chicago offers and Peter Hone's band
title: Danny Barker, the Chicago excursion and the offers Sayles turned down
summary: He recommends Danny Barker for Albert's job, tells how Barker met his uncle Paul and went to Chicago, calls it a missed break, then returns to Desvigne's band living near Randy Hall.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Yeah, had a woman piano player. I'm trying to think of her name. I know that woman well. She lived there on any street near Claiborne.
Is that Edna? No, not Edna.

No, not Edna. Willamina something. Willamina Borg. Yeah, Willamina Borg, yeah, yeah. So, uh, Danny was working up there and he hadn't so long, hadn't too long got married. And, uh, like he got married working on that job, yeah. So, he was good friends with Lee and also I was good friends with Danny, you know. So, they had a trip, this fella Sherman Cooks had a trip to, had an excursion trip to go to Chicago, you see. And, uh, Lewis Armstrong at the time was living in Chicago, you see. And, uh, Lee was telling me, man, this is my good time to get to meet my good buddy Lewis and get a chance to be around Chicago. Because, Lee had been up there before, you see. And I had, well, that was three offers I had at the same time, you know. So, I thought, I said, well, no, the best thing for me to do is go and take this job on the board. I said, I know it. If I make that season, I said, that's gonna be, you know, have a nice, but I'll get myself straightened out and do things for my wife and things. And, uh, Don Apple, I had to turn him down. So, I recommended that Danny would, would be the one to take, take the job if he wanted to, see. So, and also, um, Paul Barber was in, in Chicago with Lewis Armstrong and that, that's, uh, kind of Danny's uncle, I believe, something like that. Mm-hmm. Yeah. So, Danny wanted to see him. You see, in other words, Danny was trying to get away from here, the branch his way so he could get somewhere, you see. So, that was, uh, those were the three mistakes I made. I should have stayed there. So, those guys, they, they went to Chicago. In other words, the band went and the band got paid and the band, you know, they played a few numbers on the train. And they tell me when they got to Chicago, they even did like they did in the Orleans. They went on the truck and advertised, you know, around. And they went with Lewis and Lewis went, went with them and see, they had a ball, man. So, that's where Danny met his uncle, uh, Paul. And Paul, they must have got again and told him, say, well, you can, I can see that you, you'll get, uh, you'll get something, see if you just come on up here. And they must have been, Paul, and that time Lewis must have been figuring on going to New York, see. So, anyhow, Lewis and Paul, Paul was working with Lewis Armstrong, they didn't go to New York. And I don't know whether Danny went to Chicago or went to Winston Hill, but anyhow, it was through Paul, I think, that got him open. And then Danny went to Chicago, then maybe went to New York. Well, I didn't see Danny for a long time, boy, and I heard he'd been playing with bands like the Blue, Blue something band around New York. In other words, he had made contact with the big fellas, you see. The next thing I heard he was, excuse me, was with the, with Cab Calloway band, you see. So, like I said, I mean, that could have been a break for me, but I did make the seat with Sidney. I came back here and I stayed with Sidney band. I remember I was living on, on Prairie and La Hoppe. I was still with my first wife and Randy Hall, which became the, it was another band, young band, a fellow younger me was becoming to be a good banjo player and arranger. I was doing arranging myself in those days. I was staying with Gene Ware and his wife, Zareta, and my, me and my wife, Alma, we were staying on Prairie and La Hoppe. And Randy Hall was staying right across the street from us and they had another fellow named Reuben Hughes. In other words, it was a kind of little musician's center all staying around up in that thing, you know what I'm saying? And we all were working with Sidney. So, this thing got a little rough with Sidney and Gene had, had went and got him a job at one of the Jitney places, see. It might have been the foreign, you see. Well, then the WPA band was out, you could go join them, but I always, I was a guy like this. I said, well, I could always get out here and, and what you call, pick up or hustle a little more work, because I was working with Black Sidney band. And I'd come out here and work around Decatur Street, around French Street up in there, and when the band wasn't doing nothing, it would be like, I mean I was playing still playing banjo, like banjo and piano, and piano and piano and drumming the horn, and work maybe two or three nights a week, see. Then when the band would get something like this time here, the band would be plenty busy, you see. But like after Mardi Gras, things would drop, you see. And that's the time when we'd go around and get these little jobs. And then somehow I used to work out.
